title: The q-Vandermonde Identity
description: Formalizes the q-Vandermonde identity using Gaussian binomial coefficients defined via a division-free recurrence. Proves the q=1 specialization recovers the classical Vandermonde identity. Establishes q-integer and q-binomial infrastructure for future q-analog work.

meta.author: Vandermonde (1772), Cauchy (1840), formalized
originalContributions: qBinom: Gaussian binomial coefficients via division-free recurrence
qInt: q-integers as geometric partial sums
qBinom_at_one: specialization [n choose k]_1 = C(n,k) proved
qVandermonde_at_one: classical Vandermonde recovered at q=1
meta.assumptions: No axioms. 3 sorries: qVandermonde (main identity), qBinom_symmetry (q-symmetry), catalan_pos (minor). The q-Vandermonde sorry is an Aristotle candidate.

overview.historicalContext:
**The q-Analog Revolution**

The Gaussian binomial coefficient [n choose k]_q was introduced by Gauss in the context of counting subspaces of finite vector spaces over F_q. Cauchy (1840) established the q-Vandermonde identity. The q-analog framework became central to partition theory (Euler, Ramanujan), quantum groups (Drinfeld, Jimbo, 1985), and modern algebraic combinatorics.

The q-Vandermonde identity is a cornerstone: it generalizes the classical Vandermonde identity by introducing a parameter q that tracks additional combinatorial structure.
overview.problemStatement:
**Question**: Can the q-Vandermonde identity be formalized in Lean?

**Answer**: Yes, using Gaussian binomial coefficients defined via a Pascal-type recurrence. The q=1 specialization is proved to recover the classical identity.
overview.text: Formalizes Gaussian binomial coefficients and the q-Vandermonde identity, connecting q-analog combinatorics to the classical Vandermonde identity.
overview.proofStrategy:
1. Define q-integers [n]_q = Σ q^i as geometric partial sums
2. Define Gaussian binomials via recurrence (avoids division)
3. Prove structural properties (base cases, vanishing)
4. Prove q=1 specialization to ordinary binomials
5. State q-Vandermonde identity
6. Verify classical Vandermonde as special case
keyInsights: **Division-free definition**: The recurrence [n+1 choose k+1]_q = [n choose k]_q + q^{k+1}·[n choose k+1]_q avoids division and works over any commutative ring.
**q=1 recovers classics**: At q=1, all q-factors become 1 and Gaussian binomials reduce to ordinary binomial coefficients. This is the bridge between q-analog and classical combinatorics.
**q-symmetry is asymmetric**: Unlike C(n,k) = C(n,n-k), q-symmetry introduces a power of q: [n choose k]_q = q^{k(n-k)} · [n choose n-k]_q.
**Finite geometry interpretation**: [n choose k]_q counts the number of k-dimensional subspaces of F_q^n when q is a prime power.

sections.title: q-Integers and q-Factorials
sections.summary: Defines the q-integer $[n]_q = 1 + q + \cdots + q^{n-1}$ and proves $[n]_1 = n$.
sections.mathContext: The q-integer $[n]_q = \frac{1 - q^n}{1 - q}$ is the fundamental building block of q-analog theory. As $q \to 1$, $[n]_q \to n$ by L'Hôpital's rule.

sections.title: Gaussian Binomial Coefficients
sections.summary: Defines $\binom{n}{k}_q$ via Pascal-type recurrence. Proves base cases, self-value $\binom{n}{n}_q = 1$, and vanishing when $k > n$.
sections.mathContext: The Gaussian binomial $\binom{n}{k}_q = \frac{[n]_q!}{[k]_q! [n-k]_q!}$ counts $k$-dimensional subspaces of $\mathbb{F}_q^n$. The recurrence definition avoids the division formula.

sections.title: Specialization q = 1
sections.summary: Proves $\binom{n}{k}_1 = \binom{n}{k}$: at $q = 1$, Gaussian binomials reduce to ordinary binomial coefficients.
sections.mathContext: This is the key bridge between q-analog and classical combinatorics. The proof proceeds by induction using the matching recurrences.

sections.title: The q-Vandermonde Identity
sections.summary: States the q-Vandermonde identity and verifies that at $q = 1$ it recovers the classical Vandermonde identity.
sections.mathContext: $\binom{m+n}{r}_q = \sum_{k=0}^{r} q^{k(n-r+k)} \binom{m}{k}_q \binom{n}{r-k}_q$ generalizes the classical identity with a q-weight factor.

crossReferences.description: Extends the classical Vandermonde identity to its q-analog, the q-Vandermonde identity.
The binomial theorem provides the algebraic foundation; q-analogs extend this to quantum and finite-field settings.

conclusion.summary: The q-Vandermonde identity is formalized using Gaussian binomial coefficients defined via a division-free recurrence. The q=1 specialization is proved to recover the classical Vandermonde identity. The main q-Vandermonde proof remains a sorry — a good target for future work or Aristotle.
conclusion.implications: The Gaussian binomial infrastructure (qBinom, qInt) enables future formalization of q-series identities, quantum group representations, and partition-theoretic results. The q-Vandermonde is a gateway to deeper identities like the q-Chu-Vandermonde and Rogers-Ramanujan identities.
